label: A drawing, not a reconstruction of any section
noRunCaption: If you look into the tissue before starting a run, the staining scenes show a built-in standard run (per procedure), not saved.
noBasisCaption: Not modeled: the model has no picture for this run, so the tissue stays unstained. What is missing: {explanation}.
impregnationNotDone: The field is unstained: the ammoniacal silver bath has not been performed on this run, so the model has bound no silver yet.
developmentNotDone: Silver is bound in the model, but development has not been performed, so there is no visible silver yet. Binding is not development.
impregnationNoSilver: The ammoniacal silver bath was performed, but with this run's settings the model bound no silver, so the field stays unstained.
developmentNoSilver: Development was performed, but the model found no bound silver to reduce, so no visible silver was made: no reaction.

impregnationNotDone.text: The course procedure lists the ammoniacal silver bath before development; until that step is performed the model binds no silver.

developmentNotDone.text: A plateau in silver binding does not mean visible deposition has finished; binding and development are modeled as separate processes.

items.title: A schematic brain
items.caption: A cartoon brain built from simple shapes sits on the specimen tray. It is not an atlas; no real anatomy was traced.

items.title: A cortex patch, standing in
items.caption: A patch of cortex lights up. It stands in for the course specimens, whose species, region, fixation and thickness are unknown here.

facts.text: The species, brain region, fixation and section thickness of the course specimens are not known to this lab; the course procedure records tissue, region and thickness per slide rather than fixing them.

items.title: Cutting a section
items.caption: A plane sweeps through the patch and a thin slab lifts out. The slab's thickness is a drawing choice, not the course's.

facts.text: The course procedure does not fix a section thickness (it is recorded per slide), so the slab here has an arbitrary thickness.

items.title: One thin section
items.caption: The slab settles onto a slide. A single thin section cannot establish a true 3D reconstruction of a plaque or tangle.

facts.text: A single thin section cannot establish a true 3D reconstruction of a plaque or tangle.

items.title: Into the section
items.caption: Through the eyepiece, the camera drops into the section. Every shape from here on is a teaching drawing; counts and sizes are not measurements.

facts.text: Every output of this lab is an illustrative, qualitative simulation; a visually convincing animation is not a validated experimental predictor.

items.title: What the shapes stand for
items.caption: Five kinds of shape stand for five structures. Each cartoon shows a shape only, not what the structure is made of.

facts.text: The Bielschowsky stain impregnates both the amyloid and the neuritic components of senile plaques and reliably stains neurofibrillary tangles.

sub.title: Axon
sub.caption: Long thin tubes running through the field stand for axons.

sub.title: Plaque core
sub.caption: A cluster of spheres with a soft halo stands for a plaque core.

sub.title: Plaque neurite
sub.caption: Short tubes radiating around a core stand for the neuritic part of a plaque.

sub.title: Tangle
sub.caption: A flame shape inside a cell body stands for a tangle.

sub.title: Neuropil thread
sub.caption: Short thin threads scattered between the cells stand for neuropil threads.

items.title: Impregnation: silver binds
items.caption: Glints show where silver has bound to the tissue. Binding is not development: a plateau in binding does not mean deposition has finished.

facts.text: A plateau in silver binding does not mean visible deposition has finished; binding and development are modeled as separate processes.
The silver that the developer deposits can come from silver already bound to the tissue during impregnation or from the developing solution (Peters 1955, nerve tissue sections).

items.title: Development: nuclei, then deposit
items.caption: Dots mark silver nuclei, then each structure darkens as the model’s rules say. Darker does not mean more protein, more pathology or a better method.

facts.text: Silver staining requires reduced-silver nuclei in the section, which act as centres on which the developer deposits more silver (Peters 1955, nerve tissue sections).
Darker staining does not necessarily mean more protein, more pathology or a better method.

items.title: Toning and thiosulfate
items.caption: Gold toning turns the stain gray-black; sodium thiosulfate removes unreduced silver, so the slide stops changing. This drawing keeps its silver colour.

facts.text: The course procedure lists optional gold toning and the sodium thiosulfate fix after development, before the final washes, dehydration, clearing and mounting.
Gold toning turns the stain from brown-black to gray-black; sodium thiosulfate removes silver that was never reduced, so the slide stops changing.

items.title: What you saw
items.caption: Everything here was a drawing; any darkness came from a teaching model, not a measurement. Explore the tissue or go back to the bench.

facts.text: The course raises fixation-related carbonyls, endogenous carbonyls, reduced metals and other reduction sites as competing explanations for why these structures take silver; none is established and this clip asserts none of them.
